newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-JONES EVOKES MEMORIES OF RUDOLPH AND GRIFFITH JOYNER.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JONES EVOKES MEMORIES OF RUDOLPH AND GRIFFITH JOYNER.

text.p: Less than six months after opting for track and field ahead of basketball, Marion Jones has already evoked comparisons with Wilma Rudolph's grace and Florence Griffith Joyner's pace.

The American champion, enviably composed and assured in her first year on the European circuit, won the world 100 metres final on Sunday in 10.83 seconds, two-hundredths of a second ahead of Ukrainian Zhanna Pintussevich.
Now she has the opportunity at the sixth world championships here to emulate Rudolph and Griffith Joyner by winning three major titles at the same championships.
Eventually she could even match Jesse Owens and Carl Lewis by winning gold in the 100, 200, long jump and 4x100 relay at the Sydney 2000 Olympics.
Placing Jones alongside a quartet of the finest athletes produced by the world's greatest sprinting nations shows just how far she has come since deciding to return to athletics.
Rudolph, tall and lissome, graced the 1960 Rome Olympics with victories in the 100 and 200 followed by gold in the 4x100 metres relay.
Twenty-eight years later Griffith Joyner, in a extraordinary few months, set records in the 100 and 200 which endure to this day and matched Rudolph's medal haul at the Seoul Olympics.
Trevor Graham, who has coached Jones to the U.S. and world 100 metres titles this year, says her height, form and style are reminiscent of Rudolph.
"I can see someone saying that Marion reminds them of Wilma," Graham agreed.
Graham also believes Jones is the woman to beat Griffith Joyner's track records of 10.49 and 21.34 and Galina Chistyakova's world long jump mark of 7.52 metres, also set in 1988.
"I know she can break Flo's record," Jones said before the championships. "It's just a matter of time. I know she is going to break the world record in the long jump too, it's just a matter of time.
"I really can't put a limit on this girl, I can't."
Jones, denied a victory lap by over-zealous officials on Sunday, was asked if she believed a new era had begun in women's sprinting.
"I hope so," she replied. "I am still learning. I want to break the world (100) record. Until I do that I won't consider myself the best sprinter.
"I definitely have the potential. If everything goes right, hopefully in a few years I can.
"As a child I set goals for myself, one was the Olympic Games, one was the world championships, one was to be the fastest woman in the world.
"I am not going to stop until I reach all of those."
